title: Computational neuroscience & AI
content_html:
Computational neuroscience & AI

Computational neuroscience builds formal, often mathematical or algorithmic models of neural systems to explain how the brain processes, stores, and recalls information. Models range from very simple abstractions to biophysically realistic simulations.

Simplify a neuron into an electrical capacitor: input currents accumulate until a threshold is reached → a “spike” is fired, simple ODEs describing membrane potential. A biophysically detailed model of ion channels describes how action potentials arise from sodium/potassium conductances. This all shows how individual cells can act as threshold devices or resonate to rhythmic inputs (important for oscillatory memory dynamics).

Instead of simulating every spike, neurons are grouped into populations, modeled by firing rates. Coupled nonlinear differential equations describing excitatory and inhibitory population dynamics. Populations can settle into stable activity states = candidate “memory states”, like treating the brain as a continuous medium, rather than discrete molecules.

Fully recurrent networks of binary neurons, with symmetric weights. They store patterns as attractor states in an “energy landscape.” → Retrieval is like a ball rolling into the nearest valley. Attractor models are used to explain working memory (persistent activity loops) and episodic recall. These and other models explain how memory traces are formed, consolidated, and updated. Organisms model the world as generative dynamical systems, minimizing surprise by updating predictions (ties memory, perception, and learning together). Memory is modeled as inference under uncertainty, the brain combines prior knowledge with noisy evidence to reconstruct memories. Essentially memory lives inside a generative model that predicts inputs - it is not a perfect store but an adaptive, probabilistic reconstruction. Computational neuroscience models are diverse mathematical toolkits — from ion-channel physics to Bayesian inference — that let us describe memory as a dynamic, distributed, emergent process, much like flows in a fluid system.

Modern neuroscience increasingly borrows from artificial neural networks; transformers and recurrent nets model sequence memory and attention, whilst contrastive learning frameworks are used to simulate hippocampal encoding/recall. So the theories are bidirectional: neuroscience inspires AI, AI models inform neuroscience.

Artificial intelligence began as an attempt to imitate brain processes. Many key AI architectures come directly from neuroscience concepts, for example, the idea of units with weighted inputs and outputs. “Cells that fire together, wire together” inspired early perceptrons and later unsupervised learning rules. Hubel & Wiesel’s discovery of receptive fields (simple and complex cells in cat V1) led directly to convolution layers and hierarchical vision models Neural evidence for selective attention, gating, and context-dependent memory informed the design of attention mechanisms and memory-augmented architectures. Concepts of rhythm, replay, and top-down prediction in the brain influenced predictive coding algorithms and variational autoencoders.

The flow now runs in reverse as well: AI architectures give neuroscientists new testable models for brain function. Networks trained on vision tasks (e.g., ImageNet CNNs) generate internal representations that closely match neuronal firing patterns in primate visual cortex, which provides a “synthetic brain” to test hypotheses. Theories about how the hippocampus encodes temporal/relational memory offer candidate mechanisms for how the brain generalizes across episodes, which influences AI transformers and sequence learning. Energy landscapes in Hopfield-like models inform analyses of attractor dynamics in cortex and hippocampus. Reinforcement learning (RL) agents reveal parallels with dopamine reward systems, basal ganglia loops, and exploration/exploitation trade-offs.

The result is a virtuous cycle: Neuroscience supplies mechanisms and inspiration (cells, rhythms, circuits). AI supplies working computational models that can be trained, tested, and compared against neural data.
